clue.text: At top speed, even in the shops

blocks.note: even, level ground is flat
a new book or record that is out is available in the shops

explanation.surface: Someone rushing about at full pelt, even while doing the shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even' reads as an adverb in the surface but is an adjective meaning level.
explanation.definitionFit: Going flat out is an idiom for travelling or working as fast as possible.

clue.text: Deceitfully appease fellow, old boy on holiday

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
someone on holiday is off work

explanation.surface: A former schoolmate on vacation is being placated with a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: To fob someone off is to put them off with an excuse or a trick so that they stop complaining.

clue.text: Pulled political pamphlet showing wrong date on the outside

indicators.note: something wrong is not in its correct state, so the letters of date need fixing
a thing on the outside wraps around something else, so the jumbled date surrounds the pamphlet

blocks.note: the four letters to be rearranged
a tract is a short pamphlet arguing a political or religious case

explanation.surface: A political leaflet with the wrong date printed on its cover was withdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled' suggests a pamphlet withdrawn from circulation, but it means drawn towards.
explanation.definitionFit: Attracted means drew towards oneself, a synonym of pulled in the physical sense.

clue.text: Old unaltered haven

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
as is means in the present state, without changes

explanation.surface: A long-standing refuge that has never been changed.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is figuratively a refuge or haven of calm amid difficult surroundings.

clue.text: She told me a dreadful lie, an often-repeated situation

indicators.note: dreadful means very bad, so the words before it are in a bad state and need rearranging

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged
a story is a childish word for a lie

explanation.surface: Someone complains that she told them yet another terrible lie, as usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' seems to describe the lie but works on the four words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The same old story is an idiom for a tiresome situation that keeps happening again and again.

clue.text: Sit near suspect, crying

indicators.note: as an adjective, suspect means dubious or not sound, so the letters before it are not to be trusted in their order

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An order to take a seat beside a suspected criminal, who is weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' looks like a noun for the person you sit near, but it is an adjective telling you the letters are unsound.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in tears is the idiom for weeping, so it can stand for the adjective crying.

clue.text: I can do what I like, Italian secretary of UN snarled

definitions.text: I can do what I like

indicators.note: snarled means tangled, like a knotted line, so the words are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: It is short for Italian vermouth, a crossword staple
the thirteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An Italian official at the United Nations growls that they will do as they please.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snarled' paints an angry official, but it means tangled. The Italian and the anagram are joined end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: It's a free country is the stock retort of someone asserting their right to act as they wish.

clue.text: A few trot out love song from No, No, Nanette

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters before it are displaced

blocks.note: the eight letters to be rearranged
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: A few dancers trot out a love song from the musical No, No, Nanette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trot out' reads as a phrase meaning perform, but the anagram is a few trot, ended by the love.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea for Two is the best-known song from the 1925 musical No, No, Nanette.

clue.text: Member brought in beer, more than enough

indicators.note: brought in means taken inside, so the member goes within the drink

blocks.note: ale is a type of beer
MP stands for Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A member of a club brought in plenty of beer, more than enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful, enough or more than enough of something.

clue.text: Type, mostly for money

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a species is a kind or type

explanation.surface: A sort of thing, mostly for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Specie is money in the form of coins rather than notes, a formal word for hard cash.

clue.text: Nuts about English short-story writer

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for nuts goes around the other piece

blocks.note: bats is slang for mad
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone is crazy about a certain English writer of short fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: H. E. Bates was an English author famous for his short stories and The Darling Buds of May.
explanation.definitionFit: H. E. Bates is a well-known example of an English writer of short stories.

clue.text: Very simple? Yes, ape, as I set out

indicators.note: to set out things is to lay them out afresh, so the letters are arranged in a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A confident speaker tells an ape that a task is simple, as they lay it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy as pie is a colloquial simile for something requiring no effort at all.

clue.text: Habitual convict amongst female employees in a place in Arizona

indicators.note: amongst places one thing in the middle of the others, so it sits inside them

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
an old lag is a long-term or repeat prisoner
a workforce is its staff

explanation.surface: A repeat offender working among the women on a payroll somewhere in Arizona.
explanation.walkthrough: The convict sits between the abbreviation for female and the employees. Lag is British slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagstaff is a city in northern Arizona, so it is one example of a place in that state.

clue.text: Daggers drawn?

blocks.note: surface reading: at daggers drawn, the idiom for open hostility
setter's reading: dagger symbols drawn in print, the typographer's marks used for footnotes

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom of two people at daggers drawn pulls you towards weapons; instead the daggers are the printed marks drawn on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: The obelus is the dagger symbol used in printing, and its plural names several such marks drawn on a page.

clue.text: Exactly how rent is paid?

blocks.note: first meaning: precisely, following every detail
second meaning, whimsical: rent goes to the person who lets the property

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning reads letter as one who lets a house, the landlord, rather than a character of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Following instructions to the letter is an idiom for carrying them out precisely.

clue.text: Musician, loud-voiced bird

blocks.note: first meaning: a player of a brass instrument
second meaning: a swan or South American bird named for its loud call

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one noisy singer; the clue splits into a player and a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The name fits both a brass player and the trumpeter swan, whose call sounds like a horn.

clue.text: Decree nisi after one leaves unhappy home

indicators.note: leaves means goes away, so the letter for one is taken out of the decree
unhappy means disturbed, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the provisional divorce order, taken letter by letter
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A provisional divorce order is granted after one partner walks out of an unhappy home.
explanation.walkthrough: A decree nisi is the provisional stage of an English divorce, fitting the unhappy home of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A residence is the formal word for the place where someone lives, a house or dwelling.

clue.text: Betray Lorraine, for example

definitions.note: the clue's example names the Cross of Lorraine; the answer is the kind of cross it is

blocks.note: first meaning: to cheat someone you are supposedly working with
second meaning: the Cross of Lorraine has two horizontal bars

explanation.walkthrough: Lorraine looks like a woman being betrayed; it is the French region whose heraldic cross has two crossbars.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross with two bars is a double cross, and the Cross of Lorraine is the classic example of that design.

clue.text: Cheap cigar egoist smoked

indicators.note: smoked suggests the letters were cured and changed, so they appear in a new arrangement

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A self-important man puffed on a cheap cigar.
explanation.definitionFit: A stogie is an American term for a long thin, cheaply made cigar.

clue.text: Electrician's gear on board steamship

indicators.note: on board means aboard a vessel, so the gear sits between the two letters for the ship

blocks.note: SS is the prefix for a steamship
park is a setting on an automatic gearbox

explanation.surface: An electrician's tools are aboard a steamship.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for is, so the clue reads Electrician is gear on board steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparks is a traditional nickname for an electrician, and also for a ship's radio operator.

clue.text: Derelict carriage broken into by male

indicators.note: something broken into has an intruder inside it, so the second item goes within the first

blocks.note: a trap is a light horse-drawn carriage
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: An abandoned carriage that some man has broken into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derelict' looks like an adjective describing the carriage, but here it is a noun for a vagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: A derelict, as a noun, is a homeless destitute person, which is what a tramp is.

clue.text: Alter the last word, sixth letter in 'regards'

indicators.note: sixth letter names the exact position in the quoted word to be kept

blocks.note: amen is the closing word of a prayer, hence the last word
counting along the quoted word to its sixth character

explanation.surface: An editor changes the closing word of a letter, near the sign-off regards.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend is to make changes to a text or law in order to improve it, much as altering does.

clue.text: Forked out, defeated at college

blocks.note: to be stumped is to be baffled or beaten
a student is up at university during term

explanation.surface: Someone paid out money after being beaten while at university.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge is the British way of saying you are studying there.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump up is an informal British phrase for paying money, often reluctantly, as does forking out.

clue.text: Steel structure only demolished under pressure

indicators.note: demolished means knocked down, so the letters are broken and rebuilt
in a down entry, under places the rebuilt word below the letter for pressure

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure
the four letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A steel structure was only knocked down because of public pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: A pylon is a tall steel lattice tower that carries overhead power lines.

clue.text: Petersham, perhaps, seen in outstanding film

blocks.note: great means excellent or outstanding
a thin film or layer over a surface is a coat

explanation.surface: Someone named Petersham appears in a brilliant movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Petersham looks like a person or place, but it is a heavy overcoat named after Lord Petersham; 'film' is a layer, not a movie.
explanation.definitionFit: A petersham is a heavy woollen overcoat, so it is one example of the long thick garment worn over other clothes.

clue.text: No mixer in Martell one requested

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the brandy name, the next word and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone orders a Martell cognac neat, with no mixer added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No mixer' reads as a bar order for the brandy without a mixer; it really describes an unsociable person.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixer is a sociable person, so someone who is no mixer prefers being alone.

clue.text: Quite old, small tree on both banks of Liffey

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its two edges, so only the outside letters of the word are taken

blocks.note: the elder is a small tree or shrub bearing elderberries
the first and last letters of the Dublin river's name

explanation.surface: A rather old small tree grows along both banks of Dublin's river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Liffey is the river that runs through Dublin, which makes 'banks' natural in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly describes people past middle age, which is a polite way of saying fairly old.

clue.text: Crazy, bishop leaving after year in a city on the Hudson River

definitions.text: a city on the Hudson River

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so the bishop's letter drops out of the word for crazy
after places the trimmed word behind the abbreviation for year

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year
bonkers is slang for mad
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop goes mad and departs a Hudson River city after a year there.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonkers is a city in New York State lying on the east bank of the Hudson, just north of the Bronx.
